{{Short description|Polytope}}
The '''Birkhoff polytope''' <math>B_n</math> is the [[convex polytope]] in <math>\R^{n^2}</math> whose points are the [[doubly stochastic matrix|doubly stochastic matrices]], that is, the <math>n\times n</math> [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] whose entries are non-negative [[real number]]s and whose rows and columns each add up to 1. It is named after [[Garrett Birkhoff]], and also called the '''assignment polytope''', the '''polytope of doubly stochastic matrices''', or the '''perfect matching polytope''' of the [[complete bipartite graph]]&nbsp;<math>K_{n,n}</math><ref name="z">{{citation |last=Ziegler |first=Günter&nbsp;M. |title=Lectures on Polytopes |volume=152 |page=20 |year=2007 |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |edition=7th printing of 1st |location=New York |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-94365-7 |author-link=Günter M. Ziegler |orig-year=2006}}</ref>.

== Properties ==
===Vertices===
The Birkhoff polytope has <math>n!</math> vertices, one for each permutation on <math>n</math> items.<ref name="z"/>  This follows from the [[Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem]], which states that the [[extreme point]]s of the Birkhoff polytope are the [[permutation matrices]], and therefore that any doubly stochastic matrix may be represented as a convex combination of permutation matrices; this was stated in a 1946 paper by [[Garrett Birkhoff]],<ref>{{citation | last = Birkhoff | first = Garrett | author-link=Garrett Birkhoff |title = Tres observaciones sobre el algebra lineal [Three observations on linear algebra] | journal = Univ. Nac. Tucumán. Revista A. | volume = 5 | year = 1946 | pages = 147–151 | mr = 0020547 }}.</ref> but equivalent results in the languages of [[projective configuration]]s and of [[regular graph|regular]] [[bipartite graph]] [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]]s, respectively, were shown much earlier in 1894 in [[Ernst Steinitz]]'s thesis and in 1916 by [[Dénes Kőnig]].<ref>{{citation | last = Kőnig | first = Dénes | author-link = Dénes Kőnig | title = Gráfok és alkalmazásuk a determinánsok és a halmazok elméletére | journal = Matematikai és Természettudományi Értesítő | volume = 34 | year = 1916 | pages = 104–119}}.</ref> Because all of the vertex coordinates are zero or one, the Birkhoff polytope is an [[integral polytope]].

===Edges===
The edges of the Birkhoff polytope correspond to pairs of permutations differing by a cycle:  
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>(\sigma,\omega)</math> such that <math>\sigma^{-1}\omega</math> is a cycle. }} 
This implies that the [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] of <math>B_n</math> is a [[Cayley graph]] of the [[symmetric group]] <math>S_n</math>. This also implies that the graph of <math>B_3</math> is a [[complete graph]] <math>K_6</math>, and thus <math>B_3</math> is a [[neighborly polytope]].

===Facets===
The Birkhoff polytope lies within an {{nowrap|<math>(n^2-2n+1)</math>-dimensional}} [[affine subspace]] of the {{nowrap|<math>n^2</math>-dimensional}} space of all <math>n\times n</math> matrices. This subspace is determined by the linear equality constraints that the sum of each row and of each column must equal one. Within this subspace, it is defined by <math>n^2</math> [[linear inequality|linear inequalities]], one for each coordinate of the matrix, specifying that the coordinate must be non-negative. Therefore, for <math>n\ge 3</math>, it has exactly <math>n^2</math> [[facet (geometry)|facets]].<ref name="z"/> For <math>n=2</math>, there are two facets, given by {{nowrap|<math>a_{11}=a_{22}=0</math>,}} and {{nowrap|<math>a_{12}=a_{21}=0</math>.}}

=== Symmetries ===
The Birkhoff polytope <math>B_n</math> is both [[vertex-transitive]] and [[Isohedral figure|facet-transitive]] (i.e. the [[Dual polyhedron|dual polytope]] is vertex-transitive).  It is not [[regular polytope|regular]] {{nowrap|for <math>n > 2</math>.}}

===Volume===
An outstanding problem is to find the volume of the Birkhoff polytopes.  This has been done {{nowrap|for <math>n\le 10</math>.<ref name="beck-pixton">{{citation |last1=Beck |first1=Matthias |last2=Pixton |first2=Dennis |title=The Ehrhart Polynomial of the Birkhoff Polytope |journal=Discrete and Computational Geometry |date=1 October 2003 |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=623–637 |arxiv=math/0202267 |doi=10.1007/s00454-003-2850-8 |s2cid=7164663 }}</ref>}} It is known to be equal to the volume of a polytope associated with standard [[Young tableau]]x.<ref>{{citation |author-link=Igor Pak |first=Igor |last=Pak |title=Four questions on Birkhoff polytope |journal=[[Annals of Combinatorics]] |volume=4 |year=2000 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.1007/PL00001277|s2cid=1250478 }}.</ref> A combinatorial formula for all <math>n</math> was given in 2007.<ref>{{citation |title=Formulas for the volumes of the polytope of doubly-stochastic matrices and its faces |first1=Jesus A. |last1=De Loera|author1-link=Jesús A. De Loera |first2=Fu |last2=Liu |first3=Ruriko |last3=Yoshida|author3-link= Ruriko Yoshida |year=2007 |arxiv=math.CO/0701866 |doi=10.1007/s10801-008-0155-y |volume=30 |journal=Journal of Algebraic Combinatorics |pages=113–139|s2cid=5837937 }}.</ref>  The following [[asymptotic formula]] was found by [[Rodney Canfield]] and [[Brendan McKay (mathematician)|Brendan McKay]]:<ref>{{cite arXiv |first1=E. Rodney |last1=Canfield |author-link2=Brendan McKay (mathematician) |first2=Brendan D. |last2=McKay |title=The asymptotic volume of the Birkhoff polytope |year=2007 |eprint=0705.2422 |class=math.CO |mode=cs2}}</ref>
:<math>\mathop{\mathrm{vol}}(B_n) \, = \, \exp\left( - (n-1)^2\ln n + n^2 - \left(n - \frac{1}{2}\right)\ln(2\pi) + \frac{1}{3} + o(1) \right) .</math>
For small values <math>n\le 15</math> the volume was estimated in 2014<ref>{{citation |chapter=Efficient Random-Walk Methods for Approximating Polytope Volume |first1=Ioannis |last1=Emiris |first2=Vissarion |last2=Fisikopoulos |title=Annual Symposium on Computational Geometry - SOCG'14 |date=2014 |pages=318–327 |publisher=ACM  |doi=10.1145/2582112.2582133 |arxiv=1312.2873 |isbn=9781450325943 |s2cid=372936 }}</ref> while similar estimations follow.<ref>{{citation |last1=Cousins |first1=Ben |last2=Vempala |first2=Santosh |title=A practical volume algorithm |journal=Mathematical Programming Computation |date=2016 |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=133–160 |doi=10.1007/s12532-015-0097-z|s2cid=10365756 }}</ref>

===Ehrhart polynomial===

Determining the [[Ehrhart polynomial]] of a polytope is harder than determining its volume, since the volume can easily be computed from the leading coefficient of the Ehrhart polynomial. The Ehrhart polynomial associated with the Birkhoff polytope is only known for small values.<ref name="beck-pixton" />  It is conjectured that all the coefficients of the Ehrhart polynomials are non-negative.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}}

== Generalizations ==
*The Birkhoff polytope is a special case of the ''transportation polytope'', a polytope of nonnegative rectangular matrices with given row and column sums.<ref>{{citation |first1=V.A. |last1=Emelichev |first2=M.M. |last2=Kovalev |first3=M.K. |last3=Kravtsov |title=Polytopes, Graphs, and Optimization |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1984}}</ref>  The integer points in these polytopes are called [[contingency table]]s; they play an important role in [[Bayesian statistics]].
*The Birkhoff polytope is a special case of the ''[[matching polytope]]'', defined as a [[convex hull]] of the [[perfect matching]]s in a finite graph.  The description of facets in this generality was given by [[Jack Edmonds]] (1965), and is related to [[Edmonds's matching algorithm]].
* The Birkhoff polytope is a special case of the ''[[flow polytope]]'' of nonnegative flows through a network.<ref>{{citation |last1=Baldoni-Silva |first1=W. |last2=De Loera |first2=J. A. |last3=Vergne |first3=M. |title=Counting Integer Flows in Networks |journal=Foundations of Computational Mathematics |date=2004 |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=277–314 |arxiv=math/0303228 |doi=10.1007/s10208-003-0088-8|s2cid=2541019 }}</ref> It is related to the [[Ford–Fulkerson algorithm]] that computes the maximum flow in a flow network.
